1.1 Introduction
In accordance with the requirements of Title 10 of the Code of Federal Regulations (10 CFR)
50.10, “License required; limited work authorization,” SMR, LLC is applying, on behalf of
Palisades SMR, LLC, for a limited work authorization (LWA) to begin construction of a dual-unit
SMR-300 plant located at the Palisades Energy Center (PEC) in Covert, Michigan. The units are
individually named Pioneer Unit 1 and Pioneer Unit 2. A description of planned activities is
provided in Chapter 1 of Enclosure I of this application.
This preliminary safety analysis report (PSAR) is Enclosure II of the LWA application, which is
the first part (Part 1) of an application for a construction permit for a utilization facility under
10 CFR Part 50 to authorize the construction of a dual-unit SMR-300 plant, consisting of two
individual SMR-300 small modular reactors. Part 2 will include the remaining information to
support issuance of the construction permit and will be filed no later than 18 months after this
Part 1 submittal.
The content of this PSAR addresses only those chapters and sections of NUREG-0800,
“Standard Review Plan for the Review of Safety Analysis Reports for Nuclear Power Plants:
LWR Edition,” (SRP) [Ref. 1.1.1] that are applicable to the activities to be performed under the
LWA. As such, the numbering sequence of the LWA PSAR chapters and sections is consistent
with the SRP. For example, Chapter 3 of this LWA PSAR contains Sections 3.2, “Classification
of Structures, Systems, and Components,” 3.7,”Seismic Design,” and 3.8, “ Design of Seismic
Category I Structures.” These sections are included to support the LWA activities. Within this
PSAR, “[RESERVED]” denotes information to be provided in Part 2 of the construction permit
application or a future operating license application, and “[NOT USED]” denotes section
numbers that will not be included in licensing documentation for Pioneer Units 1 and 2.
The specific chapters and sections included in this PSAR are described in Table 1.1-1.
The level of detail provided in each of the LWA PSAR sections is informed by Regulatory
Guide (RG) 1.70 [Ref. 1.1.2] and Interim Staff Guidance DRNL-ISG-2022-01 [Ref. 1.1.3].
RG 1.206, Revisions 0 and 1, were also consulted to the extent applicable to 10 CFR Part 50,
“Domestic Licensing of Production and Utilization Facilities,” PSARs [Ref. 1.1.4, Ref. 1.1.5].

1.2 General Plant Description
The SMR-300 is a two-loop pressurized water reactor (PWR), utilizing two cold legs each with a
vertically mounted reactor coolant pump (RCP), two hot legs, and a single once-through steam
generator (OTSG) with an integral pressurizer (PZR) stacked on top of the OTSG. The plant
design is simplified relative to operating plants and incorporates passive and robust safety
systems to enhance its safety, construction, operation, and maintenance.
The SMR-300 safety systems are passive and are driven by natural forces (e.g., gravity,
conductive and convective heat transfer), with no reliance on pumps, external water, or offsite
power. The primary systems reside in the Reactor Building (RB). Within the RB, the Annular
Reservoir (AR), a large volume of water located between the Containment Enclosure Structure
(CES) and the Containment Structure (CS), is the SMR-300’s ultimate heat sink, providing
passive cooling to the containment. No operator action is required to mitigate design basis
accidents.
The following subsections describe the major structures and systems of the SMR-300.
1.2.1 Major Structures
Figure 1.2-1 provides the overall plot plan of the major structures for Pioneer Units 1 and 2.
1.2.1.1 Reactor Building
The RB refers to the integrated containment and enclosure structure for each SMR-300 unit. It
includes the CS, described in Sections 1.2.1.1.1 and 3.8.1, the CS internal structures, described
in Section 3.8.3, the CES, described in Section 1.2.1.1.2, and the AR, described in Section
1.2.1.1.3.
The RBs for both SMR-300 units reside on a common basemat that supports the two CSs along
with the southern portion of the shared Reactor Auxiliary Building (RAB), as discussed in
Sections 1.2.1.2 and 3.8.5.
Figure 1.2-2 and Figure 1.2-3 provide the general layout of the RB, including the CS, CES, AR,
and some primary structures, systems, and components (SSCs).
1.2.1.1.1 Containment Structure
The CS is partially embedded with approximately half of its height above ground level. Below
grade, the CS is made up of steel-concrete modules, called the steel-concrete containment
vessel (SCCV), which form the outer boundary of the RB. Above grade, the CS is a cylindrical
steel containment vessel (SCV) with a domed upper head. The above-grade CS is contained
within the CES. The below-grade and above-grade CS portions are joined by the Transfer
Girder (TG). The CS is a seismic Category I (SC-I) structure.
The CS contains the Reactor Pressure Vessel (RPV), Reactor Coolant System (RCS), OTSG,
Spent Fuel Pool (SFP), Passive Core Cooling System (PCC), and associated SSCs. Redundant
containment isolation valves or isolation barriers, inside and outside of the containment
boundary, are included on any fluid line that penetrates the CS.
The CS has an equipment hatch at ground level, providing access to the CS interior from the
RAB. A personnel airlock provides an additional entrance during outages and power operations.

The CS features a polar crane designed for refueling and maintenance operations, including
handling of the reactor internals and equipment needed for dry storage of spent fuel using the
Holtec International Storage Module Underground Maximum Capacity (HI-STORM UMAX)
system. A bridge crane located in the refueling/operating deck is used for fuel movements within
and between the SFP and the RPV.
1.2.1.1.2 Containment Enclosure Structure
The CES is an SC-I modular steel-concrete structure that surrounds the above-ground portion
of the CS and is designed to protect the CS from external hazards and threats. It forms the
outer wall of the AR, which provides passive containment heat removal. The CES interfaces
with the Intermediate Building (IB), which contains the main steam and main feedwater lines
upstream of their respective isolation valves and seismic restraints. The CES provides support
for these lines at the CS penetrations.
1.2.1.1.3 Annular Reservoir
The AR is contained in the annulus between the CS and CES; the CS and CES form the inside
and outside wall of the AR, respectively. A watertight seal is provided at grade level between the
CS and CES to form the bottom of the AR. The AR contains a substantial captive body of water,
and its primary function is to provide a heat sink in the event of a design basis accident.
Heat from the core may be transferred from the OTSG to the AR through the Secondary Decay
Heat Removal System (SDH) heat exchanger. Natural circulation drives flow through the heat
exchanger. Additionally, heat from the CS atmosphere may be transferred to the AR by
conduction through the steel CS wall. Heat is rejected to the atmosphere by evaporation
through the CES top vent.
1.2.1.2 Reactor Auxiliary Building
The RAB is a multi-level building adjacent to the RB (Figure 1.2-4). The RAB is shared by both
SMR-300 units of the dual-unit site. There are two main sections of the RAB. The
non-radiologically controlled area houses the Main Control Room (MCR) and the majority of the
electrical equipment and switchgear associated with the primary plant. The Radiologically
Controlled Area (RCA) contains systems to support normal primary plant operations. The RAB
is an SC-I, modular steel-concrete structure. The southern portion of the RAB (RAB-S) is
supported on a shared basemat with the CSs. The northern portion of the RAB (RAB-N) is
supported on a separate basemat at a shallower elevation.
The RCA of the RAB contains systems and equipment that are or may be radioactive or
contaminated. Major systems housed in the RCA include the Residual Heat Removal System
(RHR) , the Chemical and Volume Control System (CVC), the SFP Cooling System (SFC),
radiological waste systems, and the Remote Shutdown Facility (RSF). The Fuel Handling Area
(FHA) is also located in the RCA. The FHA includes areas for receiving, inspecting, storing, and
handling new fuel assemblies. It also includes an area to prepare spent nuclear fuel for dry
storage.
The non-radiologically controlled portion of the RAB is adjacent to the RCA. Its primary
purposes are to support the MCR and house the safety-related electrical systems. A single MCR
supports both SMR-300 units. The non-radiologically controlled area of the RAB contains the
control point for access to the RCA.

1.2.1.3 Intermediate Building
The two Intermediate Buildings (IBs) connect each RB to its associated Turbine Building (TB)
(Figure 1.2-5). The IB is a modular steel-concrete structure divided into three portions, an SC-I
structure, a seismic Category II (SC-II) structure, and a non-seismic (NS) structure. The SC-I
structure houses and supports safety-related SSCs for the Main Steam System (MSS), the Main
Feedwater System (MFS), the Steam Generator Blowdown System (SGB), and sampling
systems, including isolation valves and relief valves. The wall between the SC-I portion and the
SC-II portion has a five-way seismic restraint to ensure that failure of the SC-II structure during
a seismic event does not affect the function of the safety-related SSCs in the SC-I portion. The
SC-II and NS portions contain non-safety-related system piping.
1.2.1.4 Turbine Building
The plant includes two Turbine Buildings (TBs), each serving one power-conversion unit of the
SMR-300 plant. The TBs are connected to the non-seismic portion of the IBs (Figure 1.2-5). The
TBs are non-seismic, above-grade steel structures designed to enclose and provide weather
protection for the major turbine-generator equipment and for the laydown and maintenance
areas required to support those components. Equipment within each TB is largely unitized for its
associated power block.
Each TB houses the principal systems that support steam-cycle power generation, as discussed
in Section 10.1, including the turbine generator and main condenser. The turbine is a
down-exhaust design, with both the turbine and condenser supported on a common pedestal to
ensure alignment and accommodate operational loading. The turbine is oriented so that
potential turbine missile trajectories do not threaten safety-related plant structures or equipment.
The structural configuration of the TB uses a steel framing system with grated floors wherever
practicable, supplemented by checkered plate or reinforced concrete slab on metal deck where
required. The ground floor and the operating floor are constructed of concrete slabs. The roof
consists of metal roof panels supported by steel purlins. The building’s lateral load-resisting
system consists of horizontal and vertical bracing designed to withstand normal and severe
environmental loads, including loads experienced during construction. Structural members
exposed to mechanical and electrical support loads are designed to account for torsional
effects.
Each TB provides the necessary spatial arrangement, access platforms, and crane coverage to
support operation, inspection, and major maintenance of turbine-generator equipment. As
non-safety structures, the TBs perform no safety functions and contain no radiological shielding
features. They provide durable, weather-protected enclosures supporting the plant’s
power-conversion function throughout the design life of the SMR-300.
1.2.1.5 Electrical Building
The Electrical Building (EB) is a non-seismic reinforced concrete structure which houses SSCs
for the plant electrical distribution system. A single EB services both SMR-300 units. The EB
contains non-safety-related battery banks, instrumentation and control (I&C) cabinets,
switchgear, drives for large motors, and maintenance workshops.

1.2.1.6 Annex Building
The Annex Building is a non-seismic, traditionally framed steel structure located adjacent to the
RAB. A single building supports both SMR-300 units. The Annex Building supports plant
operational staffing including health physics, chemistry, and outage planning. Additionally, the
Annex Building serves the function of the Technical Support Center.
1.2.1.7 Water Treatment Building
The Water Treatment Building is a non-seismic steel structure which houses SSCs for the plant
water treatment systems, including the Demineralized Water Treatment System (DWT) and the
Wastewater Treatment System (WTS).
1.2.2 Major Systems
The SMR-300 core employs standard PWR fuel assemblies and utilizes rod cluster control
assemblies (RCCAs) and soluble boron to control reactivity. The core is designed for a nominal
18-month cycle length.
An SMR-300 unit includes one RPV and one OTSG connected by two hot legs and two cold
legs. The cold legs each have an RCP to drive RCS flow during normal operations. The OTSG
includes an integral PZR. All the RCS equipment, piping, and components are located inside the
CS. During normal operation, the RCPs are the driving force for flow. The RCS is configured to
facilitate natural circulation, so the RCPs are not required for decay heat removal during
accident conditions.

The Passive Containment Heat Removal System (PCH) maintains containment atmospheric
pressure and temperature within design limits in the event of a postulated accident by utilizing
conductive heat transfer between the steel CS and the water inventory in the AR. The PCH is a
completely passive system that does not require any actuations or an actuation signal to
perform its function.
Emergency core cooling is provided by four subsystems of the Passive Core Cooling System
(PCC): the Primary Decay Heat Removal System (PDH), the Secondary Decay Heat Removal
System (SDH), the Automatic Depressurization System (ADS), and the Passive Core Makeup
Water System (PCM). The PCC uses passive means such as natural circulation, gravity
injection, and compressed gas expansion for core makeup and cooling without the use of active
components such as pumps.
The SFP, located inside the CS adjacent to the RPV, is an SC-I structure sized to accommodate
discharged fuel prior to transfer into a dry storage system. The SFP includes a cask area for an
onsite shielded Holtec International Transfer Cask (HI-TRAC) that is used to deliver new fuel to
and remove spent fuel from the SFP. SFP criticality is controlled using Holtec’s patented neutron
absorber, Metamic™ in a conventional spent fuel rack geometry.

The SMR-300 power conversion systems utilize an optimized regenerative Rankine cycle with
conventional steam plant equipment. The system is designed to achieve at least 300 MWe net
generation per unit while supplying power to the plant’s house loads and includes features to
insulate the power plant from common system transients. High pressure, intermediate pressure,
and low pressure turbines are used in concert with a single turbine generator. The main
condenser is a water-cooled design; cooling water is provided by a circulating water system with
mechanical draft cooling towers.

1.4 Identification of Agents and Contractors
1.4.1 Applicant/Program Manager
For the existing Palisades Nuclear Plant (PNP) at the Palisades Energy Center (PEC), Holtec
Palisades, LLC is the plant owner, and Palisades Energy, LLC is the operator. For Pioneer Units
1 and 2 at PEC, SMR, LLC is submitting on behalf of Palisades SMR, LLC. Palisades SMR,
LLC is the proposed plant owner and anticipated holder of the limited work authorization and
construction permit, and Palisades Energy, LLC is the proposed operator. Holtec Palisades, LLC
is current the site owner of PEC.
Palisades SMR, LLC, Palisades Energy, LLC, and Holtec Palisades, LLC, are wholly owned
subsidiaries of Holtec International (Holtec), which is a technology innovation and global turnkey
project delivery company for the energy sector with a proven history since its inception in 1986.
Holtec has the capacity to design, license, manufacture, install, and operate its products,
utilizing its manufacturing facilities and global supply chain. Holtec launched its SMR-300
program a decade ago to advance nuclear power as a safe, firm power energy solution. Holtec
manages all aspects of SMR-300 program and Pioneer Units 1 and 2 project development, from
design, engineering, regulatory compliance, and business partnerships to project execution and
global market adoption. Palisades Energy, LLC, will leverage its existing operational
infrastructure, including training programs, operator qualifications, and industry memberships, to
operate Pioneer Units 1 and 2.
1.4.2 Principal Contractors and Participants
The experience and qualifications of Holtec’s agents and contractors, as well as the division of
responsibility between Holtec, its subsidiaries, its agents, and its contractors, are discussed
below.
1.4.2.1 Holtec International (Holtec)
Holtec is the reactor technology vendor and is responsible for design control of the SMR-300
and Pioneer Units 1 and 2. Holtec provides design, engineering, and technical services to PNP,
as well as design, engineering, and technical services, and nuclear grade materials and
products to the majority of the decommissioned and operating nuclear plants in the US. Holtec
has been profitable since its inception in 1986 with a proven history of turning ideas into
products that the organization delivers through an integrated project delivery structure. Holtec is
the largest exporter of capital equipment serving the global nuclear industry, 99 percent of which
is its own designs and technology. Holtec’s processes incorporate operating experience from
the design, construction, and operation of the existing fleet of pressurized light-water reactors
into the design, construction, and operation of the SMR-300 and Pioneer Units 1 and 2.
1.4.2.2 Hyundai Engineering & Construction (HDEC)
Holtec selected Hyundai Engineering & Construction (HDEC) to be its constructor and partner.
HDEC is a premier international Engineering, Procurement, and Construction (EPC) lead
selected for nuclear projects worldwide. HDEC has over 40 years of continuous nuclear power
plant construction experience in Korea and the United Arab Emirates (UAE), and a large catalog
of additional EPC contracts delivered globally. HDEC has been a fully invested partner in the
SMR-300 design and Pioneer Units 1 and 2 project since 2021, performing the balance-of-plant

1.10 Construction Impacts
1.10.1 Introduction
Pioneer Units 1 and 2 will be located at the Palisades Energy Center (PEC), the site of the
operating Palisades Nuclear Plant (PNP). Consistent with 10 CFR 50.34(a)(11), SMR, LLC
evaluated the potential impacts of construction of the Pioneer Units 1 and 2 on the systems,
structures, and components (SSCs) for the existing PNP that are safety-related or are
non-safety-related but are important to plant safety.
The applicable time period for the evaluation starts when work is first performed under the
Pioneer Units 1 and 2 limited work authorization (LWA) and ends when work is performed under
the Pioneer Units 1 and 2 full construction permit. An evaluation covering the balance of the
construction permit activities will be included in the construction permit part 2 application.
Pioneer Units 1 and 2 construction activities during the LWA period are described in Enclosure I
of the LWA application. The activities will consist mostly of below-grade construction and will not
culminate in the transition of a unit to an operational status. Therefore, the below evaluation is
limited to the construction impacts on the current PNP operating unit and does not evaluate
construction impacts on an operating SMR-300 unit.
1.10.2 Construction Impact Evaluation Plan
The construction impact evaluation identifies potential Pioneer Units 1 and 2 construction
hazards and impacts to the PNP SSCs that are safety-related or are non-safety-related but are
important to plant safety, including technical specification (TS) limiting conditions of operation
(LCOs), and proposes appropriate managerial and administrative controls to implement during
the construction activity.
The construction impact evaluation was conducted using the following steps:
   •   Identification of potential Pioneer Units 1 and 2 construction hazards
   •   Identification of PNP SSCs that are safety-related or are non-safety-related but are
       important to plant safety, including TS LCOs
   •   Identification of the subset of SSCs and TS LCOs that potentially could be impacted by
       the identified Pioneer Units 1 and 2 construction hazards
   •   Identification of applicable managerial and administrative controls to mitigate or preclude
       the potential impact of identified Pioneer Units 1 and 2 construction hazards on the
       identified subset of SSCs and TS LCOs
1.10.3 Potential Construction Activity Hazards
Pioneer Units 1 and 2 are located at the PEC in the owner controlled area generally east and
north of the PNP operating unit, as shown in Figure 1.10-1. Pioneer Units 1 and 2 are located
outside the PNP security owner controlled area (SOCA). The center of the dual-unit SMR-300
plant is approximately 2500 ft from the PNP SOCA. This separation provides a significant buffer
between the Pioneer Units 1 and 2 construction activities and the operating PNP unit and limits
the extent of SSCs and LCOs that may be impacted by Pioneer Units 1 and 2 construction
hazards.

1.10.4 Potentially Impacted SSCs and LCOs
The potential construction hazards were reviewed to identify possible impacts to PNP SSCs that
are safety-related or are non-safety-related but are important to plant safety, including TS LCOs.
The SSCs and LCOs used for this evaluation are described in the following documents.
Safety-related SSCs or non-safety-related SSCs that are important to plant safety for PNP are
identified in the PNP Updated Final Safety Analysis Report (UFSAR), Chapter 5 [Ref. 1.10.1].
Additionally, information in PNP UFSAR Chapters 3, 4, 6, 7, 8, 9, and 10 was utilized.
PNP LCOs are located in the PNP Renewed Facility Operating License, Appendix A, “Technical
Specifications,” [Ref. 1.10.2, Ref.1.10.3].
If PNP security controls are affected by potential construction hazards, the PNP Physical
Security Plan includes appropriate compensatory measures and administrative controls.
The initial assessment reviewed the previously identified PNP SSCs and LCOs to determine
whether the potential construction hazard could impact those SSCs or LCOs. Items may be
eliminated due to the applicability of the construction hazard, if they are internal to the PNP
operating unit, or are determined by examination to be sufficiently distant from the hazard that
construction impacts are not plausible. The assessment identified the subset of SSCs that could
reasonably be expected to be impacted by potential construction hazards unless administrative
and managerial controls are established. The results of the assessment are provided in

The majority of PNP safety-related SSCs and SSCs that are non-safety-related but are
important to plant safety are located within the SOCA. Based on the physical separation from
Pioneer Units 1 and 2 construction, SSCs within the SOCA will not be impacted by the Pioneer
Units 1 and 2 construction hazards.

2.1 Geography and Demography
2.1.1 Site Location and Description
Pioneer Units 1 and 2 will be constructed at the Palisades Energy Center (PEC) in Covert,
Michigan, which is also the location of the existing Palisades Nuclear Plant (PNP). This location
has been the site of a nuclear power plant since March 1971, when power generation activities
began. When in commercial operation, the power generated from Pioneer Units 1 and 2 would
be transmitted to the regional power grid through either the Midcontinent Independent System
Operator (MISO) or the Pennsylvania-New Jersey-Maryland Interconnection (PJM). The
availability of the existing power transmission infrastructure in the area is expected to minimize
the need for new power line corridor development associated with the project.
The 432-acre project site is situated on the eastern shore of Lake Michigan in a rural area of
Covert Township within Van Buren County. The project site is zoned as an Industrial District (I)
according to the Covert Township Comprehensive Zoning Ordinance Amendment, Zoning Map
[Ref. 2.1.1]. The area surrounding the project site is primarily rural and characterized by
agriculture and heavily wooded, rugged sand dunes along the lakeshore. Another electric power
plant, the Covert Generating Station, is located across Blue Star Highway immediately to the
east of the project site. Numerous recreational areas are within 50 miles of the site, with the
closest being Van Buren State Park located adjacent to the northern boundary.
An overview of the project site and planned Pioneer Units 1 and 2 layout are shown in Figure
2.1-1 and Figure 2.1-2, and associated topography is shown in Figure 2.1-3. There are existing
structures and roadways at the project site for the existing nuclear plant, some of which are
planned to be utilized in support roles for Pioneer Units 1 and 2. The offsite parcel depicted in
Figure 2.1-1 (outlined in yellow) is planned for temporary use during construction for activities
like materials laydown and assembly, concrete batching, and parking. The offsite parcel may be
converted to permanent use as a parking lot for the PEC facility.
Undeveloped areas of the project site are currently vegetated with deciduous forest covering
51.1 percent of the property, followed by grassland/herbaceous, barren land (rock/sand/clay),
and mixed forest covering approximately 12.3 percent, 11.8 percent, and 6.9 percent
respectively. Geologically, the project site is located within the Eastern Lake section of the
Central Lowlands Physiographic Province, which is characterized by low-relief surfaces formed
by glacial till, outwash plains, and glacial-lake plains.

2.5.4 Stability of Subsurface Materials and Foundations
The Pioneer Units 1 and 2 site is near the southeast shore of Lake Michigan, about 0.5 mile
inland from the lakeshore. It sits in a valley behind a shoreline ridge of sand dunes whose crests
rise more than 150 ft above lake level (Figure 2.5-1). This valley is underlain by unconsolidated
Holocene and Pleistocene deposits, which rest on thousands of feet of Paleozoic sedimentary
rock including shale, siltstone, sandstone, and limestone.
In this section, the stability of the subsurface materials on which the facility will be founded are
evaluated. The evaluation is based on understanding the regional and local geology and on the
findings of a geotechnical investigation conducted at the site in 2024. The geotechnical
investigation provides quantitative data from which to characterize the subsurface soils and rock
and assess their suitability to support the planned facility. The investigation included drilling and
logging soil and rock boreholes, installing monitoring wells, geophysical testing, and laboratory
testing of soil and rock samples.
Geotechnical and geologic characterization along with engineering analyses provide a detailed
representation of the subsurface materials as required for foundation design. The site
investigation utilized various sampling techniques at regular intervals and to sufficient depths to
provide good representation of in-situ soil conditions. Borehole spacing and locations were
selected to provide appropriate spatial coverage of the site and provide sufficient subsurface
detail to evaluate the geohazards and inform the foundation design. The site investigation
findings were used to sufficiently evaluate geohazards across the site including subsidence,
fault displacement, collapse, deformation, adverse soil conditions, and unrelieved stresses in
bedrock.
The information presented in this section has been developed in accordance with NRC
Regulatory Guides (RGs) referenced within this document and the guidance of NUREG-0800
Standard Review Plan (SRP) Section 2.5.4 [Ref. 2.5.1].
2.5.4.1 Geologic Features
This section provides a summary of the regional and local geologic setting and an
understanding of the nature and origin of the soil and rock on which Pioneer Units 1 and 2 will
be founded.
2.5.4.1.1 Regional Geology
The Pioneer Units 1 and 2 site lies in the southwest portion of the Michigan Basin, a roughly
circular intracratonic depression approximately 300 miles wide filled with a sequence of
sedimentary rocks and unconsolidated sediments up to 16,000 ft thick. The geographic center
of the Lower Peninsula of Michigan coincides with the approximate center of the basin, with its
northern edge in the Upper Peninsula of Michigan and its southern edge extending into northern
Illinois and Ohio (Figure 2.5-2) [Ref. 2.5.2, Ref. 2.5.3 ].
Continuous subsidence of the Michigan Basin during the Paleozoic Era resulted in the
deposition of a nearly complete stratigraphic sequence of marine sedimentary rocks dating from

upward, the stratigraphic section consists of Precambrian and Cambrian sandstone, Ordovician
through Devonian limestone and dolomite with lesser amounts of shale, evaporite, and
sandstone. Mississippian and Pennsylvanian shale, siltstone, sandstone, and limestone
geologic units make up the upper 10 percent of the sedimentary fill of the basin [Ref. 2.5.3].
Folding and faulting have affected the Paleozoic and older rocks in Michigan. The oldest
structural feature within the Michigan Basin is the southeast-trending arm of Precambrian
Midcontinent rift system, which extends from the Upper Peninsula of Michigan and trends
southeast beneath the Paleozoic strata of the basin (Figure 2.5-3) [Ref. 2.5.4 , Ref. 2.5.5 ,
Ref. 2.5.6].
Many northwest-southeast trending normal and reverse faults (the Lucas fault, the Sanilac fault,
and Howell Anticline) affect Paleozoic rock in the southeastern part of the State and appear to
parallel dominant fold trends in the basin. The nearest faults to the site are the Tekonsha and
Albion-Scipio trends, located 50 to 60 miles east of the site. They are northeast plunging folds
and wrench faults mapped from oil and gas drilling data in southwest Michigan [Ref. 2.5.7].
Movement is interpreted to have occurred after the Devonian and to have been associated with
subsidence of the Michigan Basin.
No active faults have been mapped in the vicinity of the site. All identified faults in the Michigan
Basin area are thought to be post Devonian to pre-Pleistocene in age, with most activity
occurring in the late Paleozoic. There is no evidence that the faults displace Pleistocene
sediment, hence these faults are not considered active.
After the Jurassic period, the Michigan Basin was uplifted and partially eroded to a landscape of
hills and streams, exposing the Paleozoic rock layers in a concentric pattern at the ground
surface (Figure 2.5-2). No depositional record exists in the Michigan Basin of the Cretaceous or
Tertiary periods.
During the Quaternary, repeated advances of continental glaciers further eroded the landscape
and left thick deposits of glacial drift and post-glacial Holocene deposits (eolian, lacustrine, and
alluvial) over the eroded bedrock surface. The thickness of the glacial deposits is variable and
exhibits lateral and vertical heterogeneity that reflects its complex depositional history
[Ref. 2.5.8, Ref. 2.5.9, Ref. 2.5.10].
Most modern landscape features (ridges, hills, plains, valleys, and lakes) in the region are the
result of glaciation that occurred in at least four distinct glacial advances, the latest known as
the Wisconsin glaciation. Wisconsin-age deposits cover much of the landscape. These deposits
include till, outwash, and glaciolacustrine deposits. Till, also known as moraine and boulder clay,
consists of a jumbled mixture of clay, silt, sand, gravel, and boulders deposited directly by the
glacier. Outwash consists of lobes or layers of sand and gravel deposited by streams draining
the glacier. Finally, glaciolacustrine deposits consist of laminated layers of silt and clay
deposited in lake waters downstream of a melting glacier.
Geologic mapping in Van Buren County near the site illustrates the distribution of these deposits
(Figure 2.5-4) [Ref. 2.5.11]. Covert Ridge, a terminal moraine 3 miles southeast of the site,
served as a dam for pro-glacial lakes during several Pleistocene lake stages. The lake stages
occurred during successive advances and retreats of the Wisconsin glacier [Ref. 2.5.3, Ref.
2.5.9], which started between 65,000 and 79,000 years ago and ended about 12,000 years ago.

2.5.4.1.2.1 Quaternary Strata
The upper strata consist of unconsolidated Quaternary deposits. They are broken into two
groups: Holocene shoreline and dune sands, and Pleistocene glacial and glacially derived
sediments (Table 2.5-1). These groups are then subdivided into stratigraphic units as described
below. Sample photographs of each Quaternary stratigraphic unit are presented in Figure 2.5-5
through Figure 2.5-9.
Holocene dune and shoreline sands date from the establishment of Lake Michigan at the close
of the Pleistocene. The Michigan lobe of the glacier retreated, and water filled the elongated
depression left behind. Wave-driven beach sands were the source for wind-driven dune sands.
Strong winds from the lake picked up the beach sand at the shore of Lake Michigan and
deposited it in inland in a mile-wide band of dunes that parallels the shore. The site is underlain
by a thick layer of dune sand that underlies the valley. To the west is a ridge of active shoreline
dunes. To the east the valley floor slopes up toward the crest of a group of smaller dunes just
beyond the site boundary (Figure 2.5-1 and 2.5-4).

2.5.4.1.4 Geologic Hazards and Adverse Conditions
Geologic conditions and features that may affect the safety of the planned facilities are reviewed
in this section. Specific geologic hazards evaluated include the potential for surface of
subsurface deformation, irregular weathering profiles and zones of weakness, unrelieved
stresses in the bedrock, unstable soils, rock mass solution cavities and discontinuities,
settlement and consolidation, liquefaction, and expansive and corrosive soils.
2.5.4.1.4.1 Surface and Subsurface Deformation
Surface deformation may occur from tectonic movements such as active faulting, from
weathering and dissolution of soluble minerals such as limestone and salt, or from slope failure.
The Pioneer Units 1 and 2 Project site is in a tectonically and seismically quiet area free of
active faults, so it is not subject to tectonic deformation. Additional discussion and evaluation of
the potential for surface deformation will be prepared in Sections 2.5.2 and 2.5.3. to be provided
in future licensing applications.
No soluble formations occur near the surface, and no karst geomorphic features, such as
sinkholes, sinking or resurging streams or dissolution caves are known in the site area. Finally,
the site is almost level, without slopes that could be subject to failure. The hazard of surface and
subsurface deformation therefore is considered low.
2.5.4.1.4.2 Irregular Weathering Profiles, Zones of Weakness
An irregular weathering profile occurs in the upper approximately 50 ft of the Coldwater Shale.
In this zone, the shale varies from completely weathered to slightly weathered. Most of the
weathering is assumed to have taken place during the Tertiary when the Coldwater Shale was
exposed to weathering and erosion at the ground surface. Portions of the soil and upper
portions of the weathered shale would have been stripped by glacial erosion during the
Pleistocene.
The completely weathered shale has strength characteristics of a silty fat clay. Slightly to
moderately weathered shale is typically characterized by beds of weak silty shale separated by
laminae of soft fat clay. Geotechnical properties of the weathered shale are presented in
Section 2.5.4.2.5.

The Pioneer Units 1 and 2 design places the foundation of the safety-related facilities within the

2.5.4.1.4.3 Unrelieved Stresses
Unrelieved stresses in the bedrock may result in creep or rebound. Stress in the Coldwater
Shale accumulated as lithostatic stress during its burial by younger Paleozoic sediments
deposited in the Michigan basin. Additional stress during this time was caused by the slow
tectonic subsidence of the Michigan Basin. Much of the lithostatic stress was relieved during the
Tertiary when erosion removed the cover sediments along with the upper 200 ft of the Coldwater
Shale.
During the Pleistocene, alternating episodes of glacial advance and retreat further eroded the
Coldwater Shale. These cycles also brought increased lithostatic stress from the weight of
approximately 3000 ft of ice during glacial periods and decreased lithostatic stress when the ice
disappeared during interglacial periods. Today the Coldwater Shale sits beneath one hundred
feet of unconsolidated Quaternary sediment, subject to the lowest lithostatic stress since its
deposition.
Given the long time (over 12,000 years) during which the Coldwater Shale has been subject to
low lithostatic stress, most of the high lithostatic stress is likely to have been relieved. The
removal of approximately 75 feet of the 110-ft thick overburden may not result in measurable
rebound or buckling. However, to ensure safety, the floor and walls of the excavation will be
continually monitored during construction.
2.5.4.1.4.4 Unstable Soils
Quaternary deposits beneath the Pioneer Units 1 and 2 site consist of unconsolidated granular
materials. These materials are stable in situ but potentially unstable during excavation if not
properly supported.
The Holocene dune and shoreline sands (sand 1 and sand 2), which comprise the upper
approximately 40 feet of the subsurface, are the most potentially unstable of these deposits.
They are loose to medium dense, uniform, poorly graded, and composed of rounded to
subrounded particles of very fine to medium quartz sand (Section 2.5.4.1.2.1). The documented
presence of shallow groundwater at the site, typically 9 to 10 ft below the ground surface,
contributes further to their potential instability. Section 2.5.4.6 provides additional groundwater
information.
The recessional deposits are expected to be more stable than the Holocene dune sands. They
are very hard and very dense and have sufficient fines content to provide cohesion. However,
beds of permeable sand occur interbedded within the recessional deposits. Water flowing
through these beds may cause piping and slope failure during excavation.
The glacial deposits are potentially the most stable of the Quaternary deposits. Typical deposits
are sandy lean clay with gravel and occasional cobbles and boulders. These deposits are very
hard and consolidated, having been overlain by the Laurentide glacier. However, interbeds of
permeable sands do occur, especially in the lower half of the glacial deposits. Water flowing
through these beds could cause piping and slope failure if excavated.

2.5.4.1.4.5 Rock Mass with Solution Cavities or Other Discontinuities
The rock beneath the Quaternary deposits at the Pioneer Units 1 and 2 site is the Coldwater
Shale of Mississippian age. Inspection of rock core during the geotechnical investigation
documented the absence of dissolution voids in this formation. Continuous beds of soluble rock
types such as limestone or dolomite were not observed in the rock core. Carbonate was present
as a secondary mineralization including calcareous cement in some fine-grained sandstone
beds, scattered dolomite concretions, and calcareous vein fillings. These carbonate features
exhibited no measurable dissolution. The hazard of solution cavities is considered low.
Discontinuities in the Coldwater Shale consist of bedding planes and joints. The bedding planes
are horizontal and closely spaced. Core samples of the shale break easily along the bedding
especially where weathered. No evidence of shearing along bedding planes was observed.
Joints are common but not abundant in the Coldwater Shale. Joints intersect the bedding at
various angles and are typically tight or healed with carbonate or silica. Open and weathered
joints were common in the weathered rock. Evidence of shearing along joint planes was
identified in fresh rock in a single borehole at 261 ft depth, where slickensides were observed
oriented down-dip on a 35-degree joint face. This shearing is attributed to Paleozoic tectonic
subsidence of the Michigan Basin.
2.5.4.1.4.6 Soil Consolidation & Settlement
Glacial deposits at the site were laid down during the latest Pleistocene when the Laurentide
glacier covered Canada and the northern United States. At its maximum extent about
18,000 years ago, the ice thickness in the Chicago area is estimated at 3,000 ft. Glacial till
deposited at the base of the glacier would have experienced significant overburden stress and
consolidation due to the weight of this ice.
As the glacier receded, the stress would have gradually been relieved. Laboratory test results,
presented in Section 2.5.4.2.4, show that both the glacial deposits and the recessional deposits
are over-consolidated.
The potential for settlement or subsidence of the ground due to soil consolidation applies to the
cohesive portion of the recessional deposits and the glacial deposits. Since both units are
overconsolidated, consolidation induced settlement is not a concern and will be accommodated
in design and construction staging. Refer to Section 2.5.4.2.4 that discusses the stress history
of fine-grained soil units. The magnitudes of consolidation settlement are presented in
Section 2.5.4.10.2.
2.5.4.1.4.7 Liquefaction Potential
Soil liquefaction is a phenomenon wherein saturated, cohesionless soils, typically loose sands,
experience a substantial loss of shear strength and stiffness due to a rapid increase in pore
water pressure, often triggered by dynamic loading such as seismic ground motion. Under these
conditions the soil behaves temporarily as a viscous fluid. This transition results in significant
ground deformation, lateral spreading, and settlement, which can compromise the stability of
foundations.

2.5.4.2.3 Engineering Properties
The subsurface investigation reveals a stratigraphic profile at the site consisting of overburden
soil overlying weathered and eroded bedrock. The overburden soil consists of two sand layers
that increase in strength and density with depth. The sand layers are underlain by lacustrine
deposits composed of laminated silt and silty clay, which overlie cohesive glacial deposits with
sandy interbeds. The overburden soil is underlain by bedrock, exhibiting a weathering profile
that decreases with depth. The degree of weathering was evaluated during drilling by the rig
geologist using standardized rock classification procedures. The detailed description of bedrock
weathering and strength characteristics is provided in Section 2.5.4.1.2.2 and 2.5.4.2.5.
Static engineering properties of the overburden soils, proposed cohesionless backfill, weathered
rock, fresh rock, and rock mass were derived from both field and laboratory testing programs.
These properties, summarized in Sections 2.5.4.2.4 and 2.5.4.2.5, support the evaluation of
stability of the foundation materials. The following sections outline the sources and
methodologies used to develop these parameters.
Based on the characterization of in-situ and laboratory results, the subsurface layers under the
NI were idealized into two soil profiles. The two profiles are identical except for the
characteristics of the glacial deposits. The first profile (profile 1) is comprised of one uniform,
cohesive glacial deposit layer, whereas the second profile (profile 2) is comprised of cohesive
glacial till overlying glacial sands, which in turn overlies a cohesive glacial till subunit. Presented
herein are the engineering properties using profile 2 stratigraphy as it encompasses all the units
in profile 1 plus the additional glacial sands.

2.5.4.2.6 Discontinuity Properties
Discontinuity data were collected through inspection and logging of rock core and by
interpretation of borehole geophysical data including acoustic and optical imaging.
These data show that most discontinuities documented in Coldwater Shale are either bedding
planes or joints that correspond to bedding planes which are referred to as “bedding joints.”
Bedding joints are closed to partially open, generally horizontal to sub-horizontal, and exhibit
smooth to slightly rough surfaces with little to no visible infill material and with dip angles
typically from 0 to 10 degrees. Where infill is present it may range in thickness from 0.02 to 1.2
in., composed of clay, calcite, dolomite or silica.
Dipping joints (10 to 90 degrees dip) that cross-cut bedding were also observed but were
significantly less common than bedding joints. These dipping joints were often healed by calcite
or silica infill, forming distinct white veins through the dark gray rock.
Discontinuity characteristics, such as roughness (Rr), weathering (Rw), and infilling (Rf), used in
rock mass characterization, were estimated as part of the rock core logging process. Numerical
values for these parameters (Rr, Rw and Rf) were assigned per borehole and elevation
intervals, based on rock mass weathering and strength properties.

2.5.4.8 Liquefaction Potential
This section presents the evaluation of liquefaction potential of the subsurface material
underlying the NI. The evaluation conforms to the guidelines of RG 1.198 [Ref. 2.5.52]. Soil
liquefaction is a geotechnical phenomenon wherein saturated, cohesionless soils, typically loose
sands, experience a substantial loss of shear strength and stiffness due to a rapid increase in
pore water pressure, often triggered by dynamic loading such as seismic ground motion. Under
these conditions, the effective stress within the soil matrix approaches zero, causing the soil to
behave temporarily as a viscous fluid. This transition results in significant ground deformation,
lateral spreading, and settlement, which can compromise the stability of foundations.
Liquefaction susceptibility is influenced by factors such as soil gradation, relative density,
confining stress, and the duration and intensity of cyclic loading.
To assess liquefaction potential, four borehole logs below the NI were evaluated. These four
logs 1) represent the range of thicknesses of sand 1 and sand 2, which are the layers deemed
to be most susceptible to liquefaction, and 2) include a profile with glacial sands to represent
idealized profile 2 and assess whether this relatively deeper sand layer is liquefiable. By
assessing each soil profile individually, the actual measured blow counts versus depth are
considered.
The blow counts versus depth measured from each of these boreholes were combined with the
other idealized soil properties to assess liquefaction. The water depth was assumed to be at 6 ft
below grade based on laboratory measurements and field observations.
Table 2.5-45 shows the seismic input parameters (i.e., peak ground acceleration (PGA) and
moment magnitude) that were used to assess liquefaction potential.

2.5.4.12 Techniques to Improve Subsurface Conditions
The presence of loose surficial sands will require ground improvement inside the nuclear island
to mitigate liquefaction, reduce settlement and increase the bearing capacity. Because the CS
and RAB structures will be founded on very dense or hard, competent soils, ground
improvement, if deemed necessary, will apply to the IB structure. Ground improvement
techniques considered include excavation and compaction of loose sands; vibro-replacement;
deep soil mixing; jet grouting; and dynamic deep compaction. These ground improvement
techniques are discussed in the following paragraphs.
2.5.4.12.1 Excavation and Backfill
Excavation and backfill are discussed in Section 2.5.4.5.
2.5.4.12.2 Vibro-Replacement
If the properties of loose sands are improved using vibro-replacement, granular columns can (1)
increase the cyclic resistance ratio by densifying the soil, (2) reduce the cyclic stress ratio by
introducing stiffer columns, and (3) dissipate excess pore water pressure quickly through the
granular columns. The increase in cyclic resistance ratio can be considered by increasing the
SPT N-value resulting from the increase in overall relative density.
Field installation will follow design drawings in terms of locations, diameters, and length of
columns. Specifications will be developed to define tolerable deviations as large deviations may
affect the performance of the foundation material. The gradation range of granular column
material and maximum particle size will be defined. In addition to installation parameters,
performance evaluation will be defined. Evaluating vibro-replacement methods in cohesionless
soils will be performed directly after installation. Soil sampling and penetration tests (such as
SPT) will be used to evaluate surrounding soils before and after ground improvement. The
degree of ground improvement or ground disturbance caused to the surrounding soils by the
ground improvement method, as well as any change in soil density, strength, and modulus will
be measured in-situ.
2.5.4.12.3 Deep Soil Mixing
For deep soil mixing, laboratory mix design tests will be performed to determine the binder
content needed to reach targeted strength. During installation, all the parameters for deep
mixing will be controlled, including binder content. After installation, the quality of the columns
will be confirmed by sampling, coring, and in-situ testing.
Data including installation records, laboratory test results and field verification tests will be
documented. Installation records will include date, time, length of column,
penetration/withdrawal rates, blade rotation rate, pressure and flow rate of injected slurry or
powder, and total slurry or powder used per column.
2.5.4.12.4 Jet Grouting
If jet grouting is utilized to improve the properties of loose sands, jet grouting records will
document grout volumes, injection pressures, rate of injection, time of injection. Additionally,
inspection of the integrity and uniformity of the grouted columns will be performed. The
dimensions of the grouted columns will be verified using in-situ testing. The grout columns will
be cored to verify strength and stiffness of the stabilized soil. In-situ tests will be performed
